extracted.intended_audience: employers, legal counsel, policymakers, worker advocates, and other stakeholders responding to or interpreting the FTC non-compete rule
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation of whether and how alternative legal and contractual tools (trade secret law, NDAs, patents, fixed-term contracts, non-solicitation clauses, competing on the merits, etc.) can adequately protect employer investments compared with non-compete agreements, and responses to public comments on those alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade secret law as a viable means of redress
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal and state trade secret laws (e.g., UTSA, DTSA, EEA) provide civil and criminal remedies for trade secret misappropriation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes injunctive relief, damages (including punitive damages), attorney's fees, ex parte seizure in extraordinary circumstances (DTSA), criminal fines and penalties (EEA), criminal or civil forfeiture, and restitution. The Commission cites high numbers of trade secret lawsuits filed annually as evidence employers commonly use these remedies and that they are a viable alternative to non-competes for protecting confidential information.

rubrics_metrics.name: NDAs (appropriately tailored) as a less-restrictive alternative
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) are contracts where a party agrees not to disclose or use information designated as confidential; when properly tailored, they protect confidential information without preventing the worker from seeking or accepting other employment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NDAs are widely used (estimates of 33%-57% of workers subject to at least one NDA) and in most States are more enforceable than non-competes. The final rule does not prevent garden-variety NDAs but prohibits NDAs that are so overbroad as to functionally prevent a worker from seeking or accepting employment or operating a business. Appropriately tailored NDAs burden competition less than non-competes because they restrict disclosure/use of information but not post-employment employment choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent law and invention assignment agreements as alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent law grants exclusive rights for a limited time to exclude others from making, using, selling, or importing an invention; invention assignment agreements give employers rights in employee-created inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a technology meets patentability standards, patent protection can be a less restrictive alternative to non-competes. Firms may choose trade secrecy over patents to avoid time-limited disclosure. Appropriately tailored invention assignment agreements further protect employer IP interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed-duration employment contracts to protect human capital investment
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers can use employment contracts with a fixed duration to ensure a worker remains employed long enough for the employer to recoup training or other up-front investments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fixed-duration terms can be set to match the period needed for cost recovery without restricting the worker's ability to work for others or start a business after employment ends. Such contracts may be entered at hiring or later in the employment relationship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competing on the merits to retain workers
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers can retain workers by improving pay, hours, working conditions, or other aspects of the job rather than using restrictive covenants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing a better job is a non-restrictive strategy to protect investments in human capital and reduce turnover; it also enlarges the pool of available labor for firms that attract talent by offering better terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-solicitation and non-recruitment agreements as targeted alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-solicitation/non-recruitment clauses restrict solicitation of clients or coworkers rather than broad post-employment work choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many workers with non-competes also face non-solicitation or non-recruitment provisions. These agreements can be narrower than non-competes but commenters noted they too can be difficult to detect and enforce; the Commission treats them as part of the suite of less-restrictive tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to show reasonable efforts to maintain secrecy (trade secret standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prevail on trade secret claims, employers generally must show they took reasonable steps to maintain the secrecy of the information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have found reasonable efforts satisfied by sharing information only among workers bound by NDAs or by maintaining information in password-protected digital spaces. The Commission rejects claims that meeting this standard requires extraordinary precautions that would impede intrafirm sharing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding overbroad NDAs that function as non-competes
rubrics_metrics.description: NDAs that are drafted so broadly that they effectively prevent a worker from seeking or accepting other employment or operating a business are prohibited by the final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The distinction between a lawful NDA and an impermissible functional non-compete depends on scope and whether the clause operates to block competitive activity; appropriately tailored NDAs remain allowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of prophylactic vs remedial protections
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether an employer needs prophylactic (prevention-based) restrictions or whether remedial tools (trade secret law, NDAs) suffice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission finds that the prophylactic feature of non-competes (blocking employment regardless of misconduct) is the source of their overbreadth; prophylactic benefits do not justify restricting competition when narrower, remedial tools exist. The availability of doctrines like inevitable disclosure in some States does not justify broad prophylactic non-competes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detectability, proof burdens, and enforcement costs of alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether alternatives (trade secret litigation, NDA enforcement) are harder to detect, prove, or more costly than enforcing non-competes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters argued enforcement under trade secret law and NDAs can be more expensive and fact-intensive; the Commission recognizes these costs but is not persuaded they render alternatives inadequate. Higher evidentiary standards help prevent overly broad restrictions on competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical and industry evidence of adequacy (state experience and litigation rates)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use empirical evidence — litigation rates, industry performance in non-enforcing States (e.g., California, North Dakota, Oklahoma) — to evaluate whether alternatives enable firms to protect investments and thrive without non-competes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission cites numbers of trade secret cases filed and the continued success of industries in States that limit non-compete enforcement as evidence that alternatives are viable. The Commission does not claim these data prove perfection but views them as relevant to adequacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to protect client relationships and goodwill through narrower tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether employer interests in client relationships and goodwill can be protected by tools other than non-competes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission suggests fixed-duration contracts, NDAs (for client lists), and competing on the merits as narrower means to protect these interests; it notes trade secret law and NDAs may not fully protect goodwill, but combined alternatives can reasonably protect employer interests while burdening competition less.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on using restrictive tools to prevent use of general trade knowledge and skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Tools should not be used to prevent a worker from using general trade knowledge and skills; such a restriction is not a legitimate interest under state common law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission states that preventing use of general skills is not legally cognizable; trade secret law and NDAs likewise cannot be used to bar general skill use, and preserving workers' ability to use skills is considered beneficial competitive activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accommodation for federal contractor personnel commitments
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider alternatives to non-competes where federal contractors need letters identifying key personnel for future contracts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission notes contractors can use fixed-term contracts or provide key personnel better jobs as alternatives to non-competes to meet contracting needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade-off between patent disclosure and duration vs trade secret protection
rubrics_metrics.description: When deciding between patent and trade secret protection, firms should weigh the time-limited exclusive rights of patents against the perpetual secrecy of trade secrets (subject to risk of disclosure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent protection gives exclusive rights for a set term but requires disclosure; firms may opt to keep an invention as a trade secret if longevity without disclosure is preferred. Patent law, together with NDAs and assignment agreements, can be part of a less-restrictive alternative package.
